page: Amazon Web Services r5a.8xlarge is a memory-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro System. It is powered by an AMD EPYC 7571 processor based on the x86_64 architecture, operating at a base frequency of 2.5 GHz. The instance configuration provides 32 virtual CPUs derived from 16 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading enabled. The memory footprint comprises 256.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, maintaining an 8.0 GB per vCPU ratio. Local storage is not bundled with this server type, requiring reliance on external network volumes, and the instance includes a baseline network bandwidth of 8 Gbps without integrated GPUs.

Benchmark data reflects clear behavioral distinctions between single-threaded and parallel execution. In single-core assessments, the AMD EPYC 7571 demonstrates lower tier throughput, scoring 590.98 on the single-core stress-ng test and 730.0 on Geekbench single-core, both placing in the bottom decile. Instruction set capabilities are limited to standard AVX, with no support for AVX-512 extensions. In contrast, multi-threaded evaluations show mid-tier output, producing a multi-core stress-ng score of 9,436.37, a PassMark CPU score of 22,396.51, and a Geekbench multi-core score of 6,270.0. Memory bandwidth results record 54.52 GB/sec for uncached read-only blocks and 26.08 GB/sec for large block writes.

From an operational perspective, the primary architectural tradeoff centers around modern compute efficiency versus memory density. The instance provides a cost-effective path to substantial memory capacity compared to Intel-based equivalents of the same generation, but its single-thread latency limits performance in serialized compute tasks. Application metrics reflect average capability across caching and storage engines, with Redis SET throughput reaching 19.63 million operations per second and database operations scoring 7,415.82 in PassMark tests.

The r5a.8xlarge is best matched with workloads that demand large in-memory capacities without requiring extreme per-core compute performance. Target operational use cases include distributed in-memory caching systems, intermediate-sized transactional or analytical relational databases, big data batch processing clusters, and enterprise memory-bound background tasks.
